sweep_summary: Wik-Mungkan (wikm1247) is in the catalog as fixed-unreviewed (initial primary, alternating secondary, weight-blind) on Kilham 1977 PL B-52 sec 3.1.3, a relay of the lost Sayers 1970a mimeo. Four title hits: (1) Sayers 1976a PL A-42 (held, sealang CC BY-SA) is first-hand and confirms on p.32 ('Normal Rhythm': first syllable stressed, strict alternation; affix classes override, p.33) though Part I is about intonation/clause stress and the Word/Foot Part II was never published; (2) Moore-Cantwell 2016 is an English-stress dissertation attached to Wik-Mungkan by a Glottolog machine mis-assignment (record says so) -- drop from the bibliography; (3) Sayers 1977 'Prosodies in some Aboriginal languages' (SIL PNG Workpapers 20, Iwaidja + Wik-Munkan) not obtainable (sil.org 403, SIL-PNG mirror lacks it, archive.org lacks vol. 20), content unknown, medium priority; (4) Sayers 1976b in Sutton (ed.) Languages of Cape York, pp.284-298, is per Ray 2021 pp.27/82 the published first-hand source that Kilham 1977 and Kilham et al. 1986 summarize, and Ray says its morpheme/word-level stress aligns with initial primary + alternating secondary; only search-only at HathiTrust (record 000126852) and lending-only at archive.org -- high priority for a library scan. Best statement read: Ray 2021 (Monash PhD, open), sec 2.4.5 pp.38-39 and 2.6.1 pp.58-61, with acoustic support, which should become the (co-)deciding modern source; coding unchanged. Nothing found contradicts the catalog.org/aiatsis/hathitrust/scholarworks 403.

new_statements.reading: Modern reference grammar, first-hand corpus analysis with four acoustic correlates (duration, F0, intensity, formants) on archival and 2015 recordings: primary stress on the first syllable, secondary on odd syllables (S.s.S.s), even syllables unstressed; reduplicated prefixes unstressed (primary on the stem); allative -ak attracts stress in even positions (supported), future vs past person suffixes differ by stress alone (partial support); two small classes (kuchek 'head', paththam 'really') take secondary stress on syllable 2 with primary still initial. Weight-blind, fixed initial; exceptions a small listed/morphological set. This confirms the catalog's classification (fixed-unreviewed, initial primary, alternating secondary) and states it more explicitly and with instrumental support than Kilham 1977's relay of the lost Sayers 1970a mimeo; note Ray treats kuchek as initial-primary + second-syllable secondary, whereas Kilham 1977 ex.11 lists it under non-initial primary, which narrows the exception set. Among the four title-hit items themselves, the best first-hand statement read is Sayers 1976a PL A-42 p.32 ('the first syllable is stressed and there is one and only one unstressed syllable between each successive stressed syllable'), which also confirms.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is not lexically contrastive; disyllables are stressed on the first syllable, trisyllables usually on the first ('the main syllable, which is usually the first'), and in longer words the first syllable carries the strongest stress with a weaker stress on the third. Departures are morphological: in compounds and verb-root + pronominal-suffix trisyllables the main accent goes to the distinguishing/qualifying element; in four-syllable two-root compounds each root syllable is accented with the main accent on the second (qualifying) word (wantya tu:ma 'wife'); in min-/mai- food compounds stress is on the second word and the first is shortened; with stem reduplication the accent falls on the last repeated syllable (the copy is unstressed).
new_statements.secondary_stress: p.374: 'In longer words the first syllable takes the strongest stress and the third syllable is weaker'; initiation-ground example: 'The main stress is on the first syllable of the qualifying word.. and the second stress is on the third syllable, which draws attention to the suffix -ma' (alternating S.s.S, as in the catalog's S.s.S.s).
new_statements.exceptions: Compounds / verb + pronominal suffix trisyllables: main accent on the qualifying element (pam tu:ma 'husband', a:k'ayka 'a place a long way off'); four-syllable two-root compounds: main accent on the second word (wantya tu:ma 'wife'); min-/mai- generic+specific food compounds: stress on the second word, first word loses final a; reduplicated stems: accent on the last repeated syllable (tya / t'tya 'he goes / goes along', tinta / tutinta 'close / very close'); long polymorphemic verbs: the main syllables of the component morphemes are emphasised and stress may point to an adverbial suffix (tennetiyaninta, p.375).
new_statements.identity_note: McConnel 1945 describes Wikmunkan (Wik-Mungkan) of the Archer, Holroyd and Edward Rivers, western Cape York Peninsula, from texts recorded in 1934 (Archer River Munkan; she notes the Holroyd River sub-group differs slightly); Sayers 1976b treats Wik-Mungkan (Wik-Munkan) as spoken at Aurukun (SIL fieldwork, 1960s-70s).

new_statements.quote: [p.91, of Aboriginal languages of Australia generally] Word stress has been considered non-contrastive, primary stress generally occurring on the first syllable and secondary stress rather more indefinitely on other syllables. || [p.92] The Foot patterns of Wik-Munkan are Ś, ŚS̆, S̆S̀, S̆S̀S̆, and S̀ (S represents syllable, ˊ primary stress, ˋ secondary stress and ˘ lack of stress). The complexity that has caused problems in describing the foot in Wik-Munkan is in relation to alternate pronunciations of words such as (a) núŋ·ăntàmăntáŋ vs. (b) núŋ···ăntàmăntàŋ 'with his/her (mother)'. In (a) each of the three feet is evenly timed, while in (b) the first foot is long, and what had been two feet in (a) now occurs as a level embedded in a second foot which is pronounced at a speed that approximately equels the first foot.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog record (initial primary, alternating secondary: initial stress) and with the existing statements from Ray 2021 and Sayers 1976a: primary stress on the first syllable, secondary stresses heading later feet (syllables 3, 5 in the example). Adds the explicit Wik-Munkan foot inventory (Ś, ŚS̆, S̆S̀, S̆S̀S̆, S̀) including a ternary foot, and the tempo-conditioned alternations (a)-(d) in which a final syllable can surface with an acute mark under even three-foot timing. It does not itself restate the word-stress rule for Wik-Munkan in a sentence; it points to Sayers 1975, 1976a, 1976b for that. Most of the paper (pp.93-99) is first-hand Iwaidja data (Sayers & Pym 1974)…
new_statements.rule_in_words: For Wik-Munkan the paper gives only the foot inventory and examples, referring to Sayers 1975/1976a/1976b for the analysis: feet are Ś (lone primary-stressed syllable), ŚS̆ (primary + unstressed), S̆S̀ and S̆S̀S̆ (unstressed syllable followed by a secondary-stressed head, optionally another unstressed), and S̀. Primary stress appears only in the word-initial foot types and every example begins with a primary-stressed first syllable (núŋ-), with later feet headed by secondary (grave) stresses, e.g. nú-ŋăn-tà-măn-táŋ = stresses on syllables 1, 3, 5. The p.91 sentence (non-contrastive word stress, primary on the first syllable, secondary less definite) is Sayers' statement of the received view for Australian languages as a class, which she does not dispute for stress placement; her point is that timing/rhythmic segmentation (feet) matters more than pitch or intensity.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary (grave) stress heads the non-initial feet S̆S̀, S̆S̀S̆ and S̀; in the worked example it falls on syllables 3 and 5 of a five-syllable inflected form. The ternary foot S̆S̀S̆ is listed but its combinatorics with the binary feet are not spelled out here (Sayers 1976a p.32 has the 'one and only one unstressed syllable between successive stressed syllables' statement).
new_statements.exceptions: Alternate pronunciations of long suffixed words: (a) three evenly timed feet núŋ·|ăntà|măntáŋ with the final syllable marked acute, vs (b) núŋ···ăntàmăntàŋ with a lengthened first foot and the remainder as two feet embedded in one foot (final syllable grave); two contracted variants (c) núŋn̆tàmn̆tàŋ and (d) núntàmtàŋ, both three evenly timed feet. Presented as timing/foot-structure variation, not as a different stress rule. No weight sensitivity or lexical exceptions are discussed in this paper.
new_statements.identity_note: The paper's Wik-Munkan material is confined to pp.91-92 (SIL entry 23644 lists subject language Wik-Mungkan [wim]); pp.93-99 report first-hand fieldwork on Iwaidja (Glottolog also tags the item N39 Iwaidja), and p.99 sec.6 mentions Pintupi, Warlpiri, Nyangumarda, Tiwi and Anindilyakwa with foot patterns ŚS, SŚ, ŚSS, SŚS for 'these languages' -- that list is not a Wik-Munkan statement. No dialect of Wik-Mungkan is singled out.

sources.quote: While there are many contrastive stress patterns for Wik-Munkan words, strong structural pressure is exerted by the pattern which I have called Normal Rhythm. This same pattern is described by Dixon (1972:274) for Dyirbal words as the 'preferred' stress pattern. In both languages the first syllable is stressed and there is one and only one unstressed syllable between each successive stressed syllable. [p.33:] ... the pressure of certain affix classes overrides Normal Rhythm. ... Part II, which is to follow, covers the following levels of the phonological hierarchy: the Word, the Foot, the Syllable and the Phoneme.

sources.quote: [p.373] Stress is not merely rhythmical; yet though it does not serve to contrast parts of speech as in English ... nevertheless accent brings out the meaning of words by stressing the significant syllables, i.e. stress falls on the root of a two-syllable word, and on the significant root syllables of a compound word. In words of two syllables stress falls on the first syllable: ... In words of three syllables stress usually falls on the main syllable, which is usually the first: ... [p.374] In longer words the first syllable takes the strongest stress and the third syllable is weaker : ... Where repetition of a stem occurs the accent falls on the last repeated syllable :
sources.locator: McConnel 1945, section 'Stress', Oceania 15(4) pp. 373-375 (pp. 101-103 of; lines 4673-4745)
sources.note: Earliest independent description (Ray 2021 p.82: disyllables initial stress, longer words initial stress with weaker stress on the third syllable, plus exceptions); independent pre-SIL confirmation of the classification.

tone.quote: [sec 2.3, p.53] Quite a number of compounds and close-knit phrases are composed of noun followed by adjective. This is the common structure of many noun phrases in Wik-Munkan, and in fact, when the adjective has the higher pitch there is no difference phonologically or in grammatical composition between close-knit noun phrases and other modified noun phrases. ... [sec 3.2, p.58] The common stress pattern of monomorphemic words is primary stress - no stress - secondary stress - no stress. ... If a vowel other than a occurs in what would normally be a no stress position, it will receive secondary stress.
tone.locator: sec 2.3 p.53; sec 3.2 pp.57-58; endnote 7 on p.71 (not p.72; note 8, pp.71-72, adds that readers give a separately written second stem 'higher pitch'); sec 4 p.58, 4.1 p.59, 4.2 p.60 ('variable stress-pitch pattern'); bibliography p.73
